items.stem: Define the term "tension".
items.answer: The pulling force exerted by a taut string, rope or cable along its length
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the pulling force exerted by a taut string, rope or cable along its length. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A stone is completely submerged and sinking at constant speed in water. Which is correct?
items.answer: Weight = upthrust + drag
items.markingKey: C. Constant velocity: forces balance.

items.stem: "Upthrust only acts on objects that float." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Any immersed object experiences upthrust; a sinking stone simply has weight greater than the upthrust.
items.markingKey: Any immersed object experiences upthrust; a sinking stone simply has weight greater than the upthrust. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A sealed container of volume 0.002 m³ is fully submerged in sea water (density 1025 kg m⁻³). Calculate the upthrust on it.
A 2.0 kg crate is on a frictionless slope at 20°. Calculate the component of its weight acting down the slope.
items.markingKey: D. F = mg sin θ (M1) = 6.71 N (A1).

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Free-body diagrams are only useful for simple textbook problems."
items.answer: They are a foundational tool used in professional engineering too, though complex systems also require numerical modelling.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they isolate one body and clarify which forces act; they underpin all engineering structural analysis. Arguments against: complex systems require many diagrams and computer models; distributed forces (pressure, drag) are idealised as single arrows. Supported judgement: They are a foundational tool used in professional engineering too, though complex systems also require numerical modelling.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "normal force"?
options: An interaction in which a system initially at rest separates into parts; total momentum stays zero while kinetic energy increases
An object remains at rest or moves with constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant external force
The resistive force exerted by a fluid on an object moving through it, opposite to the relative velocity
The contact force exerted by a surface on an object, perpendicular to the surface
items.answer: The contact force exerted by a surface on an object, perpendicular to the surface
items.markingKey: D. "normal force" is the contact force exerted by a surface on an object, perpendicular to the surface.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the tension is the same throughout a light, inextensible string passing over a frictionless pulley.
items.answer: A massless string needs no resultant force to accelerate, and a frictionless pulley exerts no tangential force, so the tension cannot change along it.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A massless string needs no resultant force to accelerate, and a frictionless pulley exerts no tangential force, so the tension cannot change along it. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Mei (mass 70 kg) stands on bathroom scales in a lift in Mumbai that is accelerating upwards at 1.2 m s⁻². Calculate the reading of the scales in newtons.
A student claims: "An object’s weight is the same on the Moon as on Earth." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Its mass is the same but weight = mg; g on the Moon is about 1.6 m s⁻², so the weight is about one-sixth.
items.markingKey: Its mass is the same but weight = mg; g on the Moon is about 1.6 m s⁻², so the weight is about one-sixth. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
This question is about free-body diagrams and types of force: weight, normal, friction, tension, drag and upthrust.

(a) Ana (mass 60 kg) stands on bathroom scales in a lift in Mumbai that is accelerating downwards at 2.0 m s⁻². Calculate the reading of the scales in newtons. [2]

(b) Explain why the normal force on a person in a lift is greater than their weight while the lift accelerates upwards. [3]

(c) "Free-body diagrams are only useful for simple textbook problems." Discuss this view, referring to the physics of free-body diagrams and types of force. [6]
items.answer: (a) 469 N (b) A resultant upward force is needed to accelerate them: N − mg = ma, so N = m(g + a) > mg. (c) They are a foundational tool used in professional engineering too, though complex systems also require numerical modelling.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] N − mg = ±ma (M1); N = 60(9.81 − 2.0) = 469 N (A1). (b) [3 marks] A resultant upward force is needed to accelerate them: N − mg = ma, so N = m(g + a) > mg. (c) [6 marks] For: they isolate one body and clarify which forces act; they underpin all engineering structural analysis. Against: complex systems require many diagrams and computer models; distributed forces (pressure, drag) are idealised as single arrows. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: They are a foundational tool used in professional engineering too, though complex systems also require numerical modelling.

items.stem: A resultant force of 12 N acts on a 3.0 kg mass. What is its acceleration?
items.answer: 4.0 m s⁻²

items.stem: Distinguish between Newton’s first law and Newton’s third law.
items.answer: The first law concerns one body: with zero resultant force its velocity is constant. The third law concerns two bodies: forces between them are equal and opposite and act on different bodies.
items.markingKey: The first law concerns one body: with zero resultant force its velocity is constant. The third law concerns two bodies: forces between them are equal and opposite and act on different bodies. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Nia writes: "When a horse pulls a cart, the cart pulls back with an equal force, so they cannot move." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The equal and opposite forces act on different bodies; the horse moves because the ground pushes it forward more than the cart pulls it back.
items.markingKey: The equal and opposite forces act on different bodies; the horse moves because the ground pushes it forward more than the cart pulls it back. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A shop sign of weight 150 N in Vienna hangs from two cables making angles of 30° and 55° with the horizontal. Calculate the tension in the cable at 30°.
items.markingKey: A. Horizontal: T₁ cos 30° = T₂ cos 55°; vertical: T₁ sin 30° + T₂ sin 55° = 150 (M1 M1); T₁ = 86.4 N (A1).

items.stem: A 2.0 kg trolley on a smooth horizontal bench is connected by a string over a pulley to a hanging mass of 1.5 kg. Calculate the tension in the string.
items.markingKey: a = m₂g/(m₁ + m₂) = 4.20 m s⁻² (M1 A1); T = m₁a = 8.41 N (A1).

items.stem: A traffic light of weight 150 N is held in equilibrium by two cables at 45° and 55° above the horizontal. Determine the tension in the cable at 55°.
items.markingKey: Resolve horizontally and vertically (M1 M1); T₂ = W cos 45°/sin(100°) = 108 N (A1).

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Newton’s laws have been replaced by Einstein’s relativity and are no longer useful."
items.answer: Newtonian mechanics remains the valid, simpler model within its domain; relativity extends rather than discards it (NOS: theories have ranges of validity).
items.markingKey: Arguments for: relativity is more accurate at high speeds and in strong gravity; GPS requires relativistic corrections. Arguments against: Newton’s laws are extremely accurate for everyday speeds; all engineering, spaceflight trajectories and sport science use them; relativity reduces to Newtonian mechanics when v ≪ c. Supported judgement: Newtonian mechanics remains the valid, simpler model within its domain; relativity extends rather than discards it (NOS: theories have ranges of validity).

items.stem:
A trolley on a friction-compensated runway is pulled by a hanging mass m. The total mass of trolley plus hanging masses is kept constant by moving masses from the trolley to the hanger. The acceleration a is measured with a light gate. Theory: mg = M_total a.

accelerating force mg / N | a / m s⁻²
0.196 | 0.189
0.392 | 0.378
0.589 | 0.562
0.785 | 0.781
0.981 | 0.985
1.177 | 1.143

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the total mass M_total of the system. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±4 %. State M_total with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) a (y) against mg (x); (b) gradient ≈ 0.992 kg⁻¹; (c) 1.01 kg; (d) (1.01 ± 0.04) kg
items.markingKey: (a) a (y) against mg (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 0.992 kg⁻¹ – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) M_total = 1/gradient = 1.01 kg (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 4 % of the value = 0.04 kg; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "An object remains at rest or moves with constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant external force"?
items.answer: Newton’s first law
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of Newton’s first law.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a larger force is needed to start a heavy trolley moving than a light one at the same acceleration.
items.answer: By F = ma, the required resultant force is proportional to mass; the heavy trolley has more inertia.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: By F = ma, the required resultant force is proportional to mass; the heavy trolley has more inertia. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A truck collides with a small car. During the collision, the force on the car from the truck is
options: smaller than the force on the truck
equal in size to the force on the truck from the car
larger than the force on the truck
items.answer: equal in size to the force on the truck from the car
items.markingKey: C. Newton’s third law; the car’s acceleration is larger because its mass is smaller.

items.stem: A 3.0 kg trolley on a smooth horizontal bench is connected by a string over a pulley to a hanging mass of 2.0 kg. Calculate the tension in the string.
items.markingKey: B. a = m₂g/(m₁ + m₂) = 3.92 m s⁻² (M1 A1); T = m₁a = 11.8 N (A1).

items.stem: A traffic light of weight 120 N is held in equilibrium by two cables at 35° and 60° above the horizontal. Determine the tension in the cable at 60°.
items.markingKey: Resolve horizontally and vertically (M1 M1); T₂ = W cos 35°/sin(95°) = 98.7 N (A1).

items.stem: A 60 kg passenger stands on a force sensor in a lift in a skyscraper. The lift accelerates upwards at 1.2 m s⁻², moves at constant speed, then decelerates at 0.8 m s⁻² to stop. (a) Calculate the sensor reading in each stage. (b) Sketch a graph of the reading against time. (c) Explain why the passenger feels "heavier" at the start. (d) State the reading if the cable broke and the lift fell freely, and explain it.
items.answer: (a) 661 N, 589 N, 541 N; (b) step up, middle level, step down; (c) the normal force exceeds the weight because a resultant upward force is required; (d) zero: passenger and lift have the same acceleration g, so no contact force is needed.
items.markingKey: (a) N = m(g + a) etc. (M1 A1 A1). (b) A1. (c) R1. (d) zero with reason (R1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The friction force that prevents surfaces in contact from sliding, which can take any value up to μₛN"?
items.answer: static friction
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of static friction.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the viscosity of oil is measured at a controlled temperature.
items.answer: Viscosity of liquids decreases strongly as temperature rises, so terminal velocities and the deduced η depend on temperature.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Viscosity of liquids decreases strongly as temperature rises, so terminal velocities and the deduced η depend on temperature. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "The friction force on a stationary block always equals μₛN." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: μₛN is the maximum; the actual static friction equals whatever is needed to prevent sliding, which may be less.
items.markingKey: μₛN is the maximum; the actual static friction equals whatever is needed to prevent sliding, which may be less. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A ball bearing of radius 1.5 mm moves at 0.02 m s⁻¹ through glycerol of viscosity 1.5 Pa s. Calculate the drag force using Stokes’ law.

Steel balls (density 7800 kg m⁻³) of different radii r are dropped into glycerol (density 1260 kg m⁻³) and their terminal velocities v are measured using marks on a tall tube. Theory: v = 2r²g(ρₛ − ρ_f)/(9η).

r / mm | v / m s⁻¹
0.50 | 0.0032
0.75 | 0.0075
1.00 | 0.0132
1.25 | 0.0197
1.50 | 0.0293
1.75 | 0.0394

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the viscosity η of the glycerol. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±3 %. State η with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) v (y) against r² in m² (x); (b) gradient ≈ 1.28 × 10⁴ m⁻¹ s⁻¹; (c) 1.11 Pa s; (d) (1.11 ± 0.03) Pa s
items.markingKey: (a) v (y) against r² in m² (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 1.28 × 10⁴ m⁻¹ s⁻¹ – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) η = 2g(ρₛ − ρ_f)/(9 × gradient) = 1.11 Pa s (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 3 % of the value = 0.03 Pa s; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: A 2.0 mm diameter steel ball (density 7800 kg m⁻³) falls through oil of density 900 kg m⁻³ and reaches a terminal velocity of 0.042 m s⁻¹. (a) Draw the forces on the ball at terminal velocity. (b) Calculate the weight and the upthrust. (c) Determine the viscosity of the oil. (d) Suggest why the measurement should be made far from the walls of the tube.
items.answer: (a) weight down; upthrust and drag up; (b) V = 4.19 × 10⁻⁹ m³, W = 3.21 × 10⁻⁴ N, U = 3.70 × 10⁻⁵ N; (c) η = (W − U)/(6πrv) = 2.84 × 10⁻⁴/(6π × 0.001 × 0.042) = 0.72 Pa s; (d) the walls disturb the flow and increase the drag, so Stokes’ law no longer applies.
items.markingKey: (a) weight down; upthrust and drag up; (b) V = 4.19 × 10⁻⁹ m³, W = 3.21 × 10⁻⁴ N, U = 3.70 × 10⁻⁵ N; (c) η = (W − U)/(6πrv) = 2.84 × 10⁻⁴/(6π × 0.001 × 0.042) = 0.72 Pa s; (d) the walls disturb the flow and increase the drag, so Stokes’ law no longer applies.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Stokes’ law"?
options: The drag on a small sphere moving slowly through a viscous fluid: F_d = 6πηrv
When body A exerts a force on body B, B exerts a force of equal magnitude and opposite direction on A, of the same type
A measure of a fluid’s resistance to flow, η, in Pa s
An interaction in which a system initially at rest separates into parts; total momentum stays zero while kinetic energy increases
items.answer: The drag on a small sphere moving slowly through a viscous fluid: F_d = 6πηrv
items.markingKey: A. "Stokes’ law" is the drag on a small sphere moving slowly through a viscous fluid: F_d = 6πηrv.

items.stem: A student in Bogotá is checking notes on static and dynamic friction and Stokes' law for drag. Which statement is incorrect?
options: The equal and opposite forces act on different bodies; the horse moves because the ground pushes it forward more than the cart pulls it back.
The change in momentum is the impulse FΔt; a large force acting for a very short time can give a small change.
Stokes’ law gives drag ∝ v for slow laminar flow; drag ∝ v² applies at higher speeds with turbulent flow.
Friction always opposes the motion of an object.
items.answer: Friction always opposes the motion of an object.
items.markingKey: D. This is incorrect: Friction opposes relative sliding between surfaces; it can cause motion, e.g. friction from the road pushes a car forward and lets you walk.

items.stem: A box slides across a floor at 5.0 m s⁻¹; the coefficient of dynamic friction is 0.25. Calculate how far it slides before stopping.
A box slides across a floor at 4.0 m s⁻¹; the coefficient of dynamic friction is 0.3. Calculate how far it slides before stopping.
"Friction is always a nuisance that engineers try to eliminate." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Friction is undesirable in some systems and essential in others; engineers control rather than eliminate it.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: friction wastes energy as heat in engines and bearings; causes wear. Arguments against: walking, braking, tyre grip and belts rely on friction; brake pads and clutches are designed for high μ. Supported judgement: Friction is undesirable in some systems and essential in others; engineers control rather than eliminate it. Markbands (15 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Which quantity is always conserved in a collision of an isolated system?
items.answer: Total momentum
items.markingKey: Total momentum (A1). No external force: momentum conserved.

items.stem: A student claims: "A large force always produces a large change in momentum." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The change in momentum is the impulse FΔt; a large force acting for a very short time can give a small change.
items.markingKey: The change in momentum is the impulse FΔt; a large force acting for a very short time can give a small change. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain how a car’s crumple zone reduces the force on passengers in a crash.
items.answer: The change in momentum is fixed by the crash; crumpling increases the collision time, so the average force F = Δp/Δt is reduced.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The change in momentum is fixed by the crash; crumpling increases the collision time, so the average force F = Δp/Δt is reduced. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A force–time graph for a kick is approximately a triangle with a peak force of 800 N lasting a total of 0.1 s. The ball has mass 5.0 kg and is initially at rest. Calculate its speed after the kick.
items.markingKey: B. Impulse = area = ½ × 800 × 0.1 = 40.0 N s (M1 A1); v = J/m = 8.00 m s⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem: A car of mass 1200 kg moving at 15 m s⁻¹ collides with a stationary car of mass 900 kg at a junction in Kuala Lumpur. They lock together. Calculate their common velocity just after the collision.
items.markingKey: Momentum conserved: 1200 × 15 = (1200 + 900)v (M1); v = 8.57 m s⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem: A force–time graph for a kick is approximately a triangle with a peak force of 200 N lasting a total of 0.05 s. The ball has mass 0.5 kg and is initially at rest. Calculate its speed after the kick.
items.markingKey: Impulse = area = ½ × 200 × 0.05 = 5.00 N s (M1 A1); v = J/m = 10.0 m s⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Airbags make cars completely safe in collisions."
items.answer: Airbags greatly reduce injury by lengthening the impact time, but they work as part of a system with seat belts and crumple zones and cannot make crashes completely safe.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they increase the stopping time and spread the force over a larger area; they significantly reduce head and chest injuries. Arguments against: they do not prevent all injuries and are less effective without seat belts; they can injure small children or out-of-position occupants; side and rear impacts are only partly protected. Supported judgement: Airbags greatly reduce injury by lengthening the impact time, but they work as part of a system with seat belts and crumple zones and cannot make crashes completely safe.

items.stem: A 0.150 kg cricket ball travelling at 32 m s⁻¹ is hit straight back at 41 m s⁻¹. The contact time is 1.2 ms. (a) Calculate the change in momentum. (b) Determine the average force on the ball. (c) Sketch a likely force–time graph and explain its shape. (d) Explain why a batter "follows through".
items.answer: (a) Δp = 0.150 × (41 + 32) = 11.0 kg m s⁻¹; (b) F = 11.0/0.0012 = 9.1 × 10³ N; (c) rises to a peak as the ball compresses then falls to zero – area = impulse; (d) following through keeps the bat in contact longer, increasing the impulse and the ball’s speed.
items.markingKey: (a) Δp = 0.150 × (41 + 32) = 11.0 kg m s⁻¹; (b) F = 11.0/0.0012 = 9.1 × 10³ N; (c) rises to a peak as the ball compresses then falls to zero – area = impulse; (d) following through keeps the bat in contact longer, increasing the impulse and the ball’s speed.

items.stem: Lars writes four statements while revising linear momentum, impulse and conservation of momentum in collisions and explosions. Which one is a misconception?
options: Any immersed object experiences upthrust; a sinking stone simply has weight greater than the upthrust.
In an elastic collision, both objects keep their original speeds.
Friction opposes relative sliding between surfaces; it can cause motion, e.g. friction from the road pushes a car forward and lets you walk.
A resultant force is only needed to change the velocity; with zero resultant force an object keeps moving at constant velocity (first law).
items.answer: In an elastic collision, both objects keep their original speeds.
items.markingKey: B. This is incorrect: Total kinetic energy is conserved, but energy and momentum are redistributed; for example a moving ball hitting an identical stationary ball stops while the other moves off.

items.stem: An egg dropped on a cushion does not break, but one dropped on concrete does, because the cushion
options: increases the time of impact, reducing the force
items.answer: increases the time of impact, reducing the force
items.markingKey: A. Same Δp, longer Δt.

items.stem: Explain the difference between elastic collisions and inelastic collisions.
items.answer: Both conserve momentum; elastic collisions also conserve total kinetic energy, while in inelastic collisions some kinetic energy is transferred to internal energy, sound or deformation.
items.markingKey: Both conserve momentum; elastic collisions also conserve total kinetic energy, while in inelastic collisions some kinetic energy is transferred to internal energy, sound or deformation. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Zara writes: "Momentum is not conserved when a ball hits a wall and stops." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The ball’s momentum is transferred to the wall and Earth; momentum of the whole system is conserved, but Earth’s velocity change is negligible.
items.markingKey: The ball’s momentum is transferred to the wall and Earth; momentum of the whole system is conserved, but Earth’s velocity change is negligible. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A rocket of mass 1.5 × 10⁵ kg on the launch pad ejects exhaust gas at 1000 kg s⁻¹ with speed 2500 m s⁻¹ relative to the rocket. (a) Use F = Δp/Δt to calculate the thrust. (b) Determine the initial acceleration. (c) Explain why the acceleration increases during the flight even if the thrust is constant. (d) Explain why F = ma cannot be applied directly to the whole flight.
items.answer: (a) 2.50 × 10⁶ N; (b) 6.86 m s⁻²; (c) the rocket mass decreases as fuel is used (and g and drag change); (d) the mass is not constant, so F = Δp/Δt must be used.
items.markingKey: (a) F = (Δm/Δt)v (M1 A1). (b) (T − mg)/m (M1 A1). (c) R1. (d) R1.

items.stem:
This question is about linear momentum, impulse and conservation of momentum in collisions and explosions.

(a) A car of mass 1500 kg moving at 12 m s⁻¹ collides with a stationary car of mass 1100 kg at a junction in Oslo. They lock together. Calculate their common velocity just after the collision. [2]

(b) Distinguish between inelastic collisions and elastic collisions. [4]

(c) Evaluate the claim: "Airbags make cars completely safe in collisions." [4]
items.answer: (a) 6.92 m s⁻¹ (b) Both conserve momentum; elastic collisions also conserve total kinetic energy, while in inelastic collisions some kinetic energy is transferred to internal energy, sound or deformation. (c) Airbags greatly reduce injury by lengthening the impact time, but they work as part of a system with seat belts and crumple zones and cannot make crashes completely safe.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] Momentum conserved: 1500 × 12 = (1500 + 1100)v (M1); v = 6.92 m s⁻¹ (A1). (b) [4 marks] Both conserve momentum; elastic collisions also conserve total kinetic energy, while in inelastic collisions some kinetic energy is transferred to internal energy, sound or deformation. (c) [4 marks] For: they increase the stopping time and spread the force over a larger area; they significantly reduce head and chest injuries. Against: they do not prevent all injuries and are less effective without seat belts; they can injure small children or out-of-position occupants; side and rear impacts are only partly protected. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: Airbags greatly reduce injury by lengthening the impact time, but they work as part of a system with seat belts and crumple zones and cannot make crashes completely safe.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "period (circular motion)".
items.answer: The time for one complete revolution, T = 2πr/v
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the time for one complete revolution, T = 2πr/v. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Yusuf writes four statements while revising circular motion: centripetal force and acceleration. Which one is a misconception?
options: Friction opposes relative sliding between surfaces; it can cause motion, e.g. friction from the road pushes a car forward and lets you walk.
Total kinetic energy is conserved, but energy and momentum are redistributed; for example a moving ball hitting an identical stationary ball stops while the other moves off.
A resultant force is only needed to change the velocity; with zero resultant force an object keeps moving at constant velocity (first law).
Centripetal force is an extra force acting on objects moving in circles.
items.answer: Centripetal force is an extra force acting on objects moving in circles.
items.markingKey: D. This is incorrect: It is not a new type of force; it is the resultant of real forces (tension, friction, gravity, normal force) acting towards the centre.

items.stem: A cyclist doubles her speed around the same circular track. Her centripetal acceleration
items.answer: increases by a factor of 4
items.markingKey: B. a = v²/r.

items.stem: A car of mass 800 kg rounds a bend of radius 100 m at 18 m s⁻¹ near Lisbon. Calculate the centripetal force needed.
The drum of a washing machine of radius 0.3 m spins at 800 revolutions per minute. Calculate the centripetal acceleration of clothes at the drum wall.

A satellite in a circular orbit 400 km above Earth’s surface has a period of 92.6 min. Radius of Earth = 6370 km. (a) Calculate the orbital speed. (b) Calculate the centripetal acceleration. (c) Identify the force providing the centripetal force. (d) Explain why astronauts on board appear weightless.
items.answer: (a) v = 2π(6.77 × 10⁶)/(5556 s) = 7.66 × 10³ m s⁻¹; (b) a = v²/r = 8.66 m s⁻²; (c) Earth’s gravitational force; (d) they and the station fall freely with the same acceleration, so there is no normal force.
items.markingKey: (a) v = 2π(6.77 × 10⁶)/(5556 s) = 7.66 × 10³ m s⁻¹; (b) a = v²/r = 8.66 m s⁻²; (c) Earth’s gravitational force; (d) they and the station fall freely with the same acceleration, so there is no normal force.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "centripetal force"?
options: A collision in which kinetic energy is not conserved, though momentum is
The resultant force on an object equals its rate of change of momentum; for constant mass F = ma
The product of force and the time for which it acts, J = FΔt, equal to the change in momentum
The resultant force towards the centre needed to keep an object moving in a circle, F = mv²/r
items.answer: The resultant force towards the centre needed to keep an object moving in a circle, F = mv²/r
items.markingKey: D. "centripetal force" is the resultant force towards the centre needed to keep an object moving in a circle, F = mv²/r.

items.stem: Explain the difference between centripetal force and centrifugal force.
items.answer: Centripetal force is the real resultant force towards the centre that causes circular motion; "centrifugal force" is an apparent outward force felt only in the rotating frame, not a real interaction.
items.markingKey: Centripetal force is the real resultant force towards the centre that causes circular motion; "centrifugal force" is an apparent outward force felt only in the rotating frame, not a real interaction. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Centripetal force is an extra force acting on objects moving in circles." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It is not a new type of force; it is the resultant of real forces (tension, friction, gravity, normal force) acting towards the centre.
items.markingKey: It is not a new type of force; it is the resultant of real forces (tension, friction, gravity, normal force) acting towards the centre. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
A rubber bung of mass 0.050 kg is whirled in a horizontal circle on a string passing through a glass tube, with a hanging mass M providing the tension. The period T is measured for different radii r. Theory: Mg = 4π²mr/T².

T / s | r / m

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the hanging mass M. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±4 %. State M with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) r (y) against T² (x); (b) gradient ≈ 1.03 m s⁻²; (c) 0.207 kg; (d) (0.207 ± 0.008) kg

items.stem: A spacecraft far from any planet switches off its engines. It will
items.answer: continue at constant velocity
items.markingKey: C. Newton’s first law.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "conservation of linear momentum"?
options: The product of mass and velocity, p = mv, a vector quantity
The total momentum of a system remains constant provided no resultant external force acts on it
A diagram showing a single object and all the external forces acting on it, drawn from the point of application
The pulling force exerted by a taut string, rope or cable along its length
items.answer: The total momentum of a system remains constant provided no resultant external force acts on it
items.markingKey: B. "conservation of linear momentum" is the total momentum of a system remains constant provided no resultant external force acts on it.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The pulling force exerted by a taut string, rope or cable along its length"?
items.answer: tension
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of tension.

items.stem: Distinguish between static friction and dynamic friction.
items.answer: Static friction acts when there is no relative sliding and adjusts up to μₛN; dynamic friction acts during sliding with a fixed value μ_d N, usually smaller.
items.markingKey: Static friction acts when there is no relative sliding and adjusts up to μₛN; dynamic friction acts during sliding with a fixed value μ_d N, usually smaller. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why banking a road allows cars to take a bend safely at higher speed.
items.answer: On a banked road the horizontal component of the normal force points towards the centre, adding to friction (or replacing it) as the centripetal force.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: On a banked road the horizontal component of the normal force points towards the centre, adding to friction (or replacing it) as the centripetal force. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student in Lima is checking notes on Newton's three laws of motion and equilibrium. Which statement is incorrect?
options: Total kinetic energy is conserved, but energy and momentum are redistributed; for example a moving ball hitting an identical stationary ball stops while the other moves off.
A heavier object falls faster because the force on it is larger.
Any immersed object experiences upthrust; a sinking stone simply has weight greater than the upthrust.
Stokes’ law gives drag ∝ v for slow laminar flow; drag ∝ v² applies at higher speeds with turbulent flow.
items.answer: A heavier object falls faster because the force on it is larger.
items.markingKey: B. This is incorrect: Its weight is larger but so is its mass; a = W/m = g is the same for all masses in the absence of drag.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about linear momentum, impulse and conservation of momentum in collisions and explosions is a common misconception? (Revision quiz set by Tariq.)
options: A resultant force is only needed to change the velocity; with zero resultant force an object keeps moving at constant velocity (first law).
The equal and opposite forces act on different bodies; the horse moves because the ground pushes it forward more than the cart pulls it back.
In an elastic collision, both objects keep their original speeds.
μₛN is the maximum; the actual static friction equals whatever is needed to prevent sliding, which may be less.
items.answer: In an elastic collision, both objects keep their original speeds.
items.markingKey: C. This is incorrect: Total kinetic energy is conserved, but energy and momentum are redistributed; for example a moving ball hitting an identical stationary ball stops while the other moves off.

items.stem: Explain the difference between weight and mass.
items.answer: Mass is the amount of matter (scalar, kg), the same everywhere; weight is the gravitational force mg (vector, N), which depends on the local field strength.
items.markingKey: Mass is the amount of matter (scalar, kg), the same everywhere; weight is the gravitational force mg (vector, N), which depends on the local field strength. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A car accelerates forwards on a road. The friction force from the road on the tyres is
items.answer: forwards
items.markingKey: D. Tyres push back on the road; the road pushes forward on the tyres.

items.stem: A 0.5 kg bucket of water is swung in a vertical circle of radius 0.6 m. At the lowest point its speed is 5.0 m s⁻¹. Calculate the tension in the rope at that point.
Two masses of 3.0 kg and 1.0 kg hang from a light string over a frictionless pulley (Atwood machine). Calculate the acceleration of the masses.
items.markingKey: D. (m₁ − m₂)g = (m₁ + m₂)a (M1 M1); a = 4.91 m s⁻² (A1).

items.stem: A rifle of mass 4.5 kg fires a 8.0 g bullet at 800 m s⁻¹. Calculate the recoil speed of the rifle.
items.markingKey: A. Total momentum zero: Mv_R = mv (M1); v_R = 1.42 m s⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem: A 0.5 kg lantern hangs from the midpoint of a wire; each half of the wire makes 40° with the vertical. Calculate the tension in the wire.
items.markingKey: 2T cos θ = mg (M1); T = 3.20 N (A1).

items.stem: The coefficient of static friction between tyres and a flat road is 0.8. Calculate the maximum speed at which a car can round a bend of radius 60 m without skidding.
items.markingKey: μmg = mv²/r (M1); v = √(μgr) = 21.7 m s⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem: Two horizontal forces of 80 N and 60 N act at right angles on a 10 kg puck on frictionless ice. Calculate the magnitude of its acceleration.
items.markingKey: Resultant = √(80² + 60²) = 100 N (M1); a = 10.0 m s⁻² (A1).

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Airbags make cars completely safe in collisions."
items.answer: Airbags greatly reduce injury by lengthening the impact time, but they work as part of a system with seat belts and crumple zones and cannot make crashes completely safe.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they increase the stopping time and spread the force over a larger area; they significantly reduce head and chest injuries. Arguments against: they do not prevent all injuries and are less effective without seat belts; they can injure small children or out-of-position occupants; side and rear impacts are only partly protected. Supported judgement: Airbags greatly reduce injury by lengthening the impact time, but they work as part of a system with seat belts and crumple zones and cannot make crashes completely safe.

items.stem: A helium balloon of volume 0.012 m³ and total mass 4.0 g is held by a string. Density of air = 1.20 kg m⁻³. (a) Draw a free-body diagram for the balloon. (b) Calculate the upthrust. (c) Determine the tension in the string. (d) Calculate the initial acceleration if the string is cut.
items.answer: (a) upthrust up, weight and tension down; (b) U = ρVg = 1.20 × 0.012 × 9.81 = 0.141 N; (c) T = U − mg = 0.141 − 0.0392 = 0.102 N; (d) a = 0.102/0.004 = 25 m s⁻² (initially, before drag acts).
items.markingKey: (a) upthrust up, weight and tension down; (b) U = ρVg = 1.20 × 0.012 × 9.81 = 0.141 N; (c) T = U − mg = 0.141 − 0.0392 = 0.102 N; (d) a = 0.102/0.004 = 25 m s⁻² (initially, before drag acts).

items.stem:
This question is about static and dynamic friction and Stokes' law for drag.

(a) A box slides across a floor at 6.0 m s⁻¹; the coefficient of dynamic friction is 0.4. Calculate how far it slides before stopping. [2]

(b) With the help of a specific example, explain why anti-lock brakes (ABS) can stop a car in a shorter distance than locked wheels. [3]

(c) Evaluate the claim: "Friction is always a nuisance that engineers try to eliminate." [4]
items.answer: (a) 4.59 m (b) Rolling tyres grip using static friction, whose maximum μₛN exceeds the dynamic friction μ_d N of skidding tyres; ABS keeps the wheels just below the slipping point. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (c) Friction is undesirable in some systems and essential in others; engineers control rather than eliminate it.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] a = μg = 3.92 m s⁻² (M1); s = u²/(2a) = 4.59 m (A1). (b) [3 marks] Rolling tyres grip using static friction, whose maximum μₛN exceeds the dynamic friction μ_d N of skidding tyres; ABS keeps the wheels just below the slipping point. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (c) [4 marks] For: friction wastes energy as heat in engines and bearings; causes wear. Against: walking, braking, tyre grip and belts rely on friction; brake pads and clutches are designed for high μ. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: Friction is undesirable in some systems and essential in others; engineers control rather than eliminate it.

items.stem:
This question is about circular motion: centripetal force and acceleration.

(a) A 0.2 kg bucket of water is swung in a vertical circle of radius 0.8 m. At the lowest point its speed is 4.0 m s⁻¹. Calculate the tension in the rope at that point. [3]

(b) With the help of a specific example, explain why banking a road allows cars to take a bend safely at higher speed. [3]

(c) Evaluate the claim: "Artificial gravity in a rotating space station would feel identical to gravity on Earth." [6]
items.answer: (a) 5.96 N (b) On a banked road the horizontal component of the normal force points towards the centre, adding to friction (or replacing it) as the centripetal force. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (c) Rotation can mimic gravity, but only a large, slowly rotating station would feel close to Earth gravity; differences remain.
items.markingKey: (a) [3 marks] T − mg = mv²/r (M1); T = 4.00 + 1.96 = 5.96 N (A1). (b) [3 marks] On a banked road the horizontal component of the normal force points towards the centre, adding to friction (or replacing it) as the centripetal force. items.stem: Define the term "Newton’s third law".
items.answer: When body A exerts a force on body B, B exerts a force of equal magnitude and opposite direction on A, of the same type
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: when body A exerts a force on body B, B exerts a force of equal magnitude and opposite direction on A, of the same type. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A collision in which kinetic energy is not conserved, though momentum is"?
items.answer: inelastic collision

options: along the tangent at the point of release
items.answer: along the tangent at the point of release
items.markingKey: A. No centripetal force; first law.

items.stem: Explain, using Newton’s laws, why passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes suddenly.
items.answer: The braking force acts on the bus, not directly on passengers; by inertia (first law) their bodies continue forward until friction from seats or the floor provides a resultant force to decelerate them.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The braking force acts on the bus, not directly on passengers; by inertia (first law) their bodies continue forward until friction from seats or the floor provides a resultant force to decelerate them. items.answer: 2mv
items.markingKey: C. Direction reverses.

items.stem: Freya and a classmate in Oslo disagree about free-body diagrams and types of force: weight, normal, friction, tension, drag and upthrust. Which statement is correct?
options: A heavier object falls faster because the force on it is larger.
If the string of a whirling ball breaks, the ball flies radially outwards.
Any immersed object experiences upthrust; a sinking stone simply has weight greater than the upthrust.
The friction force on a stationary block always equals μₛN.
items.answer: Any immersed object experiences upthrust; a sinking stone simply has weight greater than the upthrust.
items.markingKey: C. The other options are common misconceptions. Any immersed object experiences upthrust; a sinking stone simply has weight greater than the upthrust.

items.stem: A ballistic pendulum is used to measure the speed of an air-rifle pellet. A 10 g pellet embeds in a 2.0 kg wooden block hanging on strings, and the block rises by 12 cm. (a) Calculate the speed of the block just after impact. (b) Determine the speed of the pellet. (c) Calculate the percentage of the pellet’s kinetic energy that is converted to internal energy. items.answer: (a) 1.53 m s⁻¹; (b) 308 m s⁻¹; (c) 99.5 %; (d) the collision is inelastic – kinetic energy is transferred to internal energy and sound, so only momentum is conserved during the impact.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Free-body diagrams are only useful for simple textbook problems."
items.answer: They are a foundational tool used in professional engineering too, though complex systems also require numerical modelling.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they isolate one body and clarify which forces act; they underpin all engineering structural analysis. Arguments against: complex systems require many diagrams and computer models; distributed forces (pressure, drag) are idealised as single arrows. Supported judgement: They are a foundational tool used in professional engineering too, though complex systems also require numerical modelling. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.
